sections.h2: Selling a house in Hamilton Township, Atlantic County
sections.html:
Expect three steps to decide how fast a sale moves here: a resale inspection arranged through the township, a clear tax payoff, and a deed recorded at the courthouse in Mays Landing. This page is about the Atlantic County township around Mays Landing, not the Hamilton near Trenton.

The township has an estimated 28,845 residents, up 5.0 percent from 2020. About 70.7 percent of homes are owner-occupied, with a typical value of $246,200. Listings run from suburban streets in the developed east to rural lots in the pine forest of the west. A buyer paying cash for the house as it stands takes loan approval and repair haggling off the calendar. Owners with a worn-out house or a firm deadline often choose that route.

Hamilton Township covers 110.90 square miles, the most land of any New Jersey municipality. A great deal of it is protected. The township belongs to the New Jersey Pinelands National Reserve, and the Pinelands Commission regulates the western three-quarters, which remains pine forest. The eastern quarter is a Regional Growth Area where development is allowed, and most residents live there near the Hamilton Mall and other shopping centers.

Mays Landing, the county seat, sits inside the township along with McKee City and Mizpah. If your house is on or near undeveloped land, ask the township planning and zoning office whether the parcel lies inside the Pinelands Area before you tell a buyer what could be added or built.

The average home here was billed $5,931 in 2025, on a general tax rate of 3.520 per $100. Treat the table as a rough starting point and then compare recent sales of houses like yours before you name a price.

The effective rate for the township is 2.179, which is the general rate adjusted for how assessments compare with market value. Sales prices run well above assessments here, so an assessment is a poor guide to what a buyer will pay.

Before a house is resold or reoccupied, a township fire inspector tests its smoke and carbon monoxide detectors. You request the visit through the online title transfer inspection portal on the Fire Prevention page. The state Uniform Fire Code requires a smoke alarm certificate for one-family and two-family houses that are sold, leased or reoccupied, and only the municipality issues it.

The construction office at the township hall, 6101 Thirteenth Street in Mays Landing, schedules its own inspections in person or by fax and does not take requests by phone. A certificate stays valid for six months, so ask for the inspection once you have a contract and a closing date.

  • Working smoke alarms on each floor, the basement included, and near sleeping areas.
  • A carbon monoxide alarm where the code calls for one.
  • Sealed ten-year smoke alarms when you replace old ones.

Code Enforcement also responds to property maintenance complaints, so clear any open issue before you list.

The Atlantic County Board of Taxation, 5909 Main Street in Mays Landing, hears appeals. Your petition has to be in hand before the close of business at 4 p.m. on April 1, because a postmark does not count. Petitions about added or omitted assessments follow the same rule on December 1.

The board accepts filings online through MyNJAppeal.com, where evidence can be uploaded until seven days before the hearing. Assessment cards usually arrive in late January, and the board publishes lists of usable comparable sales. The test is whether your assessment exceeds what the house would sell for.

Request a payoff figure from the township tax collector before closing, and look the parcel up in the county's property assessment search before you set a price.

sections.h2: Seller costs and where the deed is filed
sections.html:
The seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee when the deed is recorded, starting at $2.00 per $500. The settlement sheet from your closing attorney or title company shows the exact charge.

The Atlantic County Clerk records deeds at the Historic Court House Complex, 5901 Main Street in Mays Landing, which lies inside the township. A satellite office serves Atlantic City at 1333 Atlantic Avenue. Make recording and transfer fee checks out to the Atlantic County Clerk's Office, and send any nonresident Gross Income Tax prepayment to the State of New Jersey Division of Taxation.

  • GIT/REP-3 residency certification for New Jersey residents.
  • Gross Income Tax prepayment for nonresident sellers, set at 2 percent of the price or more.
  • A deed prepared by the closing attorney or title company.

sections.h2: Getting from contract to closing with a cash buyer
sections.html:
With no lender in the deal, what remains is paperwork the township and county control. Start by ordering the smoke alarm inspection and fixing whatever it flags. Next, get a payoff figure from the tax collector so the title company knows what to clear out of your proceeds. Last, sign the deed and the residency or prepayment forms with the closing attorney, who files the deed with the clerk in Mays Landing.

Without an appraisal or underwriting, timing depends mostly on how soon the inspection is booked and whether the title is clean. Bring your deed, a recent tax bill, any mortgage payoff statement and the keys. Selling as is does not remove the inspection requirement, so plan for it even if you intend to make no repairs.

Back taxes get paid out of your proceeds at the table, so you need not pay them first. A failed alarm usually means a cheap battery or unit swap, followed by a reinspection. Tell any buyer when the certificate was issued, since the six months run from that date.

Before the closing date, confirm with the closing attorney that the payoff letter, the deed and the GIT forms are all ready. Missing paperwork, not the house, is what most often pushes a closing back a week or two.

A 14-mile stretch of the Atlantic City Expressway crosses the township with three interchanges, and U.S. Routes 40 and 322 and Route 50 cover other directions. NJ Transit buses 502 and 553 reach Atlantic City. Commuters care about those links, so mention them when you talk to buyers.

faqs.q: Is an inspection mandatory before selling in Hamilton Township, Atlantic County?
faqs.a: Yes. Township fire inspectors check smoke and carbon monoxide detectors before resale, and requests go through the online title transfer inspection portal. State law requires the certificate for one-family and two-family houses.

faqs.q: Where does a Hamilton Township deed get recorded?
faqs.a: At the Atlantic County Clerk's Office, 5901 Main Street in Mays Landing, inside the township. A satellite office is at 1333 Atlantic Avenue in Atlantic City.

faqs.q: What is the assessment appeal deadline here?
faqs.a: April 1 at 4 p.m., with December 1 as the date for added or omitted assessments. Filing works online, and a postmark does not satisfy the deadline.

faqs.q: Is this the same Hamilton as the one in Mercer County?
faqs.a: No. They are separate municipalities in different counties, each with its own tax board, clerk and inspection office. This page covers the one around Mays Landing.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house that sits in the Pinelands?
faqs.a: Yes. Pinelands rules govern what can be built, so ask the township planning and zoning office what the parcel's zone allows before you advertise additions or lot splits.
